Data race in [@ TLSTransportLayer::Close] (missing socket thread check) causes double-release and use-after-free

## Vulnerability: Unsynchronized `nsCOMPtr` access in `TLSTransportLayer::Close()` → double-release → UAF

**NOTE: Verifier rejected on security-boundary grounds (trigger requires chrome-privileged JS). This report documents the memory corruption defect that exists in the target file; severity is acknowledged as sub-critical (privilege-escalation primitive, not RCE).**

### Root cause

`TLSTransportLayer::Close(nsresult)` at **TLSTransportLayer.cpp:506-539** has **no thread check** — unlike the constructor/destructor which assert `OnSocketThread()`, and unlike the `Release()` method which dispatches to the socket thread via `DispatchRelease()`. The function directly mutates `nsCOMPtr` members:

Concurrently, the socket thread runs:

### Race → double-release

`nsCOMPtr::operator=(nullptr)` (nsCOMPtr.h:593→314): `T* old = mRawPtr; mRawPtr = nullptr; if (old) old->Release();`
`nsCOMPtr` move-ctor (nsCOMPtr.h:401): `this->mRawPtr = src.mRawPtr; src.mRawPtr = nullptr;` — **no AddRef** (transfer)

Interleaving:
| Step | Thread | Action |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | Main | `old = mRawPtr` → `old = cb` |
| S1 | Socket | `callback.mRawPtr = mRawPtr` → `callback = cb` |
| M2 | Main | `mRawPtr = nullptr` |
| S2 | Socket | `mRawPtr = nullptr` (redundant) |
| M3 | Main | `cb->Release()` ← −1 |
| — | Socket | `callback->OnInputStreamReady(...)` (possible UAF if M3 hit 0) |
| S3 | Socket | `callback` dtor: `cb->Release()` ← **−1 extra** |

Net: **two Releases for one owned reference** → refcount underflow.

### Victim object

`cb` = `nsStreamCopierOB` (from `NS_AsyncCopy(data->mSocketIn, pipeOut, gSocketTransportService, NS_ASYNCCOPY_VIA_WRITESEGMENTS)` at nsHttpConnectionMgr.cpp:2747). At steady state ~2-3 refs.

Firefox doesn't treat cookie name prefixes as case-insensitive

Steps to reproduce:

Hi there, I'm sorry if this is not the right location to report this.

"draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-13" (Cookies: HTTP State Management Mechanism) [1] says at "5.4. Cookie Name Prefixes":

User agents' requirements for cookie name prefixes differ slightly
from servers' (Section 4.1.3) in that UAs MUST match the prefix
string case-insensitively.

The normative requirements for the prefixes are detailed in the
storage model algorithm defined in Section 5.6.

This is because some servers will process cookie case-insensitively,
resulting in them unintentionally miscapitalizing and accepting
miscapitalized prefixes.

For example, if a server sends the following Set-Cookie header field

Set-Cookie: __SECURE-SID=12345

to a UA which checks prefixes case-sensitively it will accept this
cookie and the server would incorrectly believe the cookie is subject
the same guarantees as one spelled __Secure-.

(This section is present since draft version 11 ("draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-11"), published on 2022-11-07.)

One such example of a server/framework is ASP.NET Core, where a code like

context.Request.Cookies.TryGetValue("__Secure-SID", ...)

will also return a cookie whose name is "__SECURE-SID", "__secure-SID" etc.

However, I noticed Firefox Nightly (version 126.0a1 (2024-04-13)) seems to still treat the cookie prefixes "__Host-" and "__Secure-" as case-sensitive. For example, if I send the following header in a HTTP response (with the correct "__Secure-" prefix):

Set-Cookie: __Secure-SID=123456; path=/; samesite=lax; httponly

then Firefox correctly rejects the cookie as it's missing the "secure" attribute, as shown in the warning logged to the console:

Cookie “__Secure-SID” has been rejected for invalid prefix.

However, if I send the following header in the HTTP response:

Set-Cookie: __secure-SID=123456; path=/; samesite=lax; httponly

Heap use-after-free in [@ nsHttpHeaderArray::GetOriginalHeader] via mInVisitHeaders re-entrancy guard reset

nsHttpHeaderArray::GetOriginalHeader iterates mHeaders and, for each matching entry, passes const nsCString& references that point directly into the mHeaders nsTArray element storage to the virtual nsIHttpHeaderVisitor::VisitHeader callback. When the visitor is JS-implemented (nsXPCWrappedJS), nsXPCWrappedJS::CallMethod first performs JS_GetPropertyById on the method name (XPCWrappedJSClass.cpp:818) and only afterwards converts the C++ reference arguments via XPCConvert::NativeData2JS (line 869). A JS accessor getter on the visitHeader property therefore executes while raw pointers into mHeaders are still pending conversion.

nsHttpResponseHead protects this path with an mInVisitHeaders flag checked in SetHeader, but the flag is a plain bool guarded by a RecursiveMutex, not a re-entrancy counter. GetOriginalHeader and VisitHeaders both unconditionally write mInVisitHeaders=true on entry and mInVisitHeaders=false on exit. A nested VisitHeaders call made from inside the outer GetOriginalHeader's getter therefore resets the flag to false on return, disarming the guard for the remainder of the outer call. Subsequent SetHeader calls succeed, AppendElement reallocates mHeaders, and when CallMethod proceeds to NativeData2JS it dereferences the freed nsCString (IsVoid() reads the freed mDataFlags), yielding a heap UAF read whose value then drives string construction.

The vulnerable functions are reachable through scriptable nsIHttpChannel (HttpBaseChannel::GetOriginalResponseHeader / VisitResponseHeaders / SetResponseHeader forward 1:1 to nsHttpResponseHead). The same non-reentrant bool pattern exists in nsHttpResponseHead::VisitHeaders, nsHttpRequestHead::VisitHeaders and ReplacedHttpResponse, so all of these guards can be disarmed the same way.

Heap buffer overflow in [@ nsStandardURL::Resolve] — parent process, via forged StandardURLParams accepted by nsStandardURL::Deserialize (compromised content process, PHttpChannel)

nsStandardURL::Deserialize (/firefox/netwerk/base/nsStandardURL.cpp:3647-3749), which validates StandardURLParams received over IPC from content processes, has an incomplete relational check between the ref and path segments. It requires that the byte before mRef is '#' and that mRef is a sub-segment of mPath, but a zero-length ref positioned exactly at mPath.mPos satisfies both while placing the '#' at mPath.mPos - 1 — inside the authority rather than the path. A compromised content process can therefore make the parent accept the URI spec "[link] with authority=(7,15) ("127.0.0.1:8888#"), path=(22,1) ("/"), and ref=(22,0).

nsStandardURL::Resolve (same file, lines 2306-2515) assumes the parser-established invariant that the '#' preceding mRef lies within mPath. When the parent follows an HTTP redirect to the deprecated same-scheme relative form "Location: http:" (empty path after the scheme), Resolve computes len = mRef.mPos - 1 = 21, allocates a 22-byte result buffer via AppendToSubstring(0, 21, "") (allocation at line 1038), then sets resultPath = result + mPath.mPos = result + 22 — one byte past the allocation — and dereferences it at line 2492. ASAN reports a heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 1 in the parent process. If the out-of-bounds byte happens to be '/' (attacker-influenceable via heap grooming), net_CoalesceDirs(resultPath) is invoked on the out-of-bounds pointer and performs in-place reads and writes — escalating to an OOB write primitive. This is parent-process memory corruption fully driven by a compromised content process plus an attacker-controlled HTTP server, i.e. a sandbox-escape primitive.

Heap-use-after-free in [@ HttpChannelParent::CleanupBackgroundChannel] via re-entrant DeleteChannel from destructor

### Bug Title
Heap-use-after-free in [@ HttpChannelParent::CleanupBackgroundChannel] via nested [@ BackgroundChannelRegistrar::DeleteChannel] re-entry

### Summary

A compromised content process can drive the parent process into a state where a single `PHttpChannel::__delete__` message causes `BackgroundChannelRegistrar::DeleteChannel` to re-enter itself through the destructor of a stored `HttpChannelParent`. Because [`PLDHashTable::RawRemove`]([link] calls `clearEntry` **before** `MarkFree`, the nested lookup finds the same slot; because [`~RefPtr`]([link] does not null `mRawPtr`, the nested `clearEntry` calls `Release()` again on the same object; and because [`NS_IMPL_RELEASE`]([link] stabilizes `mRefCnt = 1` before `delete this`, the nested `Release()` sees a refcount of 1 and calls `delete this` a **second** time. The inner `operator delete` frees the object while the outer destructor is still on the stack, and the outer `CleanupBackgroundChannel` continues at line 284 reading `mAsyncOpenBarrier` from freed memory. The outer destructor's eventual `operator delete` is a double-free.

**Affected file:** [`netwerk/protocol/http/HttpChannelParent.cpp`]([link] line 279 (re-entrant trigger) and line 284 (UAF read)
**Root cause:** `CleanupBackgroundChannel` deletes `mChannels[ChannelId]` by **shared key** without verifying the entry points to `this`, and [`BackgroundChannelRegistrar::DeleteChannel`]([link] drops the stored `RefPtr` under `clearEntry`, allowing the destructor to re-enter while the slot is still findable.

### Affected Code

**File:** [`netwerk/protocol/http/BackgroundChannelRegistrar.cpp`]([link] line 58

[`nsRefCountedHashtable::Remove(aKey, nullptr)`]([link] skips `forget()` and goes straight to `RemoveEntry(ent)` → `RawRemove` → `clearEntry` → `~RefPtr` → `Release()`.

Heap-use-after-free in [@ nsUDPOutputStream::Write] via dangling PRFileDesc after UDPSocket close

### Summary

Heap-use-after-free in the parent process. [`nsUDPOutputStream`]([link] stores a raw `PRFileDesc* mFD` pointer copied from `nsUDPSocket::mFD` at construction time. The subsequent `NS_AsyncCopy` dispatches work to the Socket Transport Service thread which calls `nsUDPOutputStream::Write` → `PR_SendTo(mFD, ...)`. If `nsUDPSocket::CloseSocket()` runs on STS first (via `RecvClose` → `OnMsgClose`), it calls `PR_Close(mFD)` which frees the 48-byte `PRFileDesc` struct. The pending `Write` then dereferences the dangling pointer.

### Affected Code

**File:** [`netwerk/base/nsUDPSocket.cpp`, line 1280]([link]

**File:** [`netwerk/base/nsUDPSocket.cpp`, line 133]([link]

**File:** [`netwerk/base/nsUDPSocket.cpp`, line 768]([link]

The `nsUDPOutputStream` class ([nsUDPSocket.h:110]([link] stores `PRFileDesc* mFD` as a raw pointer. There is no synchronization or lifetime management between `CloseSocket()` freeing the FD and pending async copy operations using it. The `mIsClosed` flag on `nsUDPOutputStream` is only set by `nsUDPOutputStream::Close()`, not by the socket's `CloseSocket()`.

### Correct Pattern

Alternatively, `CloseSocket()` should cancel/close all pending `nsUDPOutputStream` instances before calling `PR_Close`.

1. Compromised content process sends `PUDPSocket::Bind` IPC → parent creates `nsUDPSocket`, allocates `PRFileDesc` via `PR_Socket`

`TransactionObserver::OnDataAvailable()` (`netwerk/protocol/http/AlternateServices.cpp`) can experience an integer overflow and subsequent underallocation and write beyond bounds (WBB) under specific conditions. The data written beyond bounds is unmodified attacker-provided data, and it is written into the heap of the chrome process.

For a request whose TLS 1.3 early data, or 0-RTT, is accepted, we currently [stamp connectEnd at full-handshake completion]([link] and then [clamp requestStart up to that value]([link] This adds roughly one handshake round trip to both connectEnd and requestStart, hiding the latency win that 0-RTT is meant to expose. Per the Fetch spec’s “record connection timing info” algorithm, when a request is sent as early data, `connectEnd` must exclude the time spent waiting to receive the server’s ServerHello: [link] So for accepted 0-RTT, `connectEnd` should be the time when the early-data request bytes are sent, and `requestStart` should be that same timestamp, not full-handshake completion.

### Summary

A compromised content process can send an arbitrary `profilePath` to the parent via the `PBackgroundStorage` IPDL constructor. The parent process opens a SQLite database from this attacker-controlled path with no validation. Because mozStorage registers its custom `like()` function without the `SQLITE_DIRECTONLY` flag and does not disable `SQLITE_TRUSTED_SCHEMA`, a malicious database can contain a VIEW that invokes `likeCompare()` during the automatic `SELECT ... FROM webappsstore2` query in `InitDatabase()`. The `likeCompare()` function at [storage/mozStorageSQLFunctions.cpp:96]([link] has a missing bounds check in CASE 4: it dereferences `*aStringItr` without checking `aStringItr != aStringEnd`, causing a heap-buffer-overflow read when the pattern is longer than the string and matches the allocation slack bytes.

### Affected Code

**File 1:** [`storage/mozStorageSQLFunctions.cpp`]([link] line 96

The outer loop is bounded only by `aPatternItr != aPatternEnd`. CASE 2 checks `aStringItr == aStringEnd` before dereferencing, but CASE 4 does not. If the pattern characters keep matching bytes beyond the string's end (null terminator and heap slack), the iterator walks into the ASAN redzone.

**File 2:** [`storage/mozStorageSQLFunctions.cpp`]([link] lines 233-236

The `like` function is registered without `SQLITE_DIRECTONLY`, allowing it to be invoked from VIEWs, triggers, and CHECK constraints in attacker-supplied database schemas.

**File 3:** [`dom/storage/StorageDBThread.cpp`]([link] lines 210-219

**File 4:** [`dom/storage/StorageIPC.cpp`]([link] line 1543

The parent only asserts in debug builds — release builds accept the constructor unconditionally.

IndexedDB database ordering leak in Firefox Private Browsing via indexedDB.databases() leads to cross-origin tracking

PoC.html

Steps to reproduce:

### Overview

In Firefox Private Browsing mode, the ordering returned by `indexedDB.databases()` is derived from process-scoped state and remains **stable, deterministic, and unique** for the lifetime of the Firefox process.

Because this ordering is not origin-scoped, unrelated origins can observe the same permutation and derive a shared identifier. The identifier also persists after all Private Browsing windows are closed (until full browser restart).

This effectively exposes process-scoped state to web content, which should not be observable under the same-origin policy.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Host the PoC page on two different origins (e.g. `origin-a.example` and `origin-b.example`).
2. Open Firefox Private Browsing.
3. Visit `origin-a.example/poc.html` and note the database ordering.
4. Visit `origin-b.example/poc.html`.
→ The same permutation will be observed (**cross-origin identifier**).
5. Close all Private Browsing windows, then open a new Private Browsing window.
6. Visit either origin again and observe the returned database ordering.
→ The same permutation persists (**same-origin identifier across private windows**).

Actual results:

- The ordering returned by `indexedDB.databases()` is identical across unrelated origins.
- The ordering remains stable across tabs and origins.
- The ordering persists even after all Private Browsing windows are closed, as long as the Firefox process is still running.

### In short
This behavior exposes process-scoped state to web content, enabling cross-origin identification that violates the same-origin isolation model and circumvents Firefox’s Enhanced Tracking Protection.

Expected results:

- The result of `indexedDB.databases()` should not expose process-scoped state across origins.

Private repository not removed on browser shutdown when PBM autostart is enabled

Originally reported by a 김도훈_5791 to the Tor Project (tracked by [this issue]([link]

If a website uses IndexDB in a private browsing window, the storage files are encrypted with a key kept in RAM only, and put in a directory named `private`.
This directory gets removed as soon as the PB window is closed.
Unfortunately, if the `browser.privatebrowsing.autostart` preference is `true` (Tor Browser's default) the `private` directory and its content are kept in place after browser's shutdown.

Steps to reproduce:

1. On a clean Firefox profile, set browser.privatebrowsing.autostart to true and restart the browser
2. Navigate to [link]
3. Verify that a $PROFILE_DIR/storage/private has been created with encrypted db files inside
3. Quit Firefox

Actual result: the $PROFILE_DIR/storage/private is still there with its content

Actually retrieving data from the encrypted database or even knowing which website it belongs requires searching a frozen snapshot of the RAM for the decryption keys, kept there during the browsing session. Furthermore you could always end in this situation if the browser just crashes, or if a determined and resourceful attacker manages to recover the encrypted files from the persistent storage after deletion.
Nonetheless I think we want this deletion policy to work as reliably as possible in global PBM as well, for consistency sake if nothing else.

## General information about TSan reports

### Why fix races?

Data races are undefined behavior and can cause crashes as well as correctness issues. Compiler optimizations can cause racy code to have unpredictable and hard-to-reproduce behavior.

### Rating

If you think this race can cause crashes or correctness issues, it would be great to rate the bug appropriately as P1/P2 and/or indicating this in the bug. This makes it a lot easier for us to assess the actual impact that these reports make and if they are helpful to you.

### False Positives / Benign Races

Typically, races reported by TSan are not false positives [1], but it is possible that the race is benign. Even in this case it would be nice to come up with a fix if it is easily doable and does not regress performance. Every race that we cannot fix will have to remain on the suppression list and slows down the overall TSan performance. Also note that seemingly benign races can possibly be harmful (also depending on the compiler, optimizations and the architecture) [2][3].

Updating if an origin is accessed on the in-memory object is not guaranteed to be done before shutting down storage

I found this while running [`originInit.js`]([link] with my patches in the verify mode (more accurately in the chaos mode).

The test cases basically create a normal cache origin and then check files in the testing cache directory.
In short, the steps roughly are:
1. Running a script with some normal cache operations.
2. Resetting.
3. Checking files.
4. Initializing.
5. Checking files again.

In step 4, I expected that the testing origin should be initialized (In other words, [`InitOrigin`]([link] should be called).

However, actually, in some extreme cases, that `InitOrigin` wasn't called and thus some test cases fail because of that.

After looking into it, I think what happened was:
a. In step 1, on the Background thread, [Cache registers a directory lock]([link]
b. In step 2, on the Background thread, [the Reset operation registers a directory lock]([link] and [it waits for the blocking lock in step 1 to be released]([link]
c. In steps 2, after [the lock is destructed]([link] on the IO thread, [the Reset operation shuts down the storage]([link] and then [writes whether the origin is accessed into database]([link]
d. In steps 2, on the Background thread, [the access time and if the origin has been accessed are updated]([link] when [unregistering the directory lock]([link]
e. In step 4, on the Background thread, [it only initializes the origins that are marked as accessed]([link]

In general case, the sequence is like: a->b->d>c->e.
However, it's possible to be like: a->b->c->d->e. It's possible that [the origin isn't marked as accessed on the Background thread]([link] before shutting down the storage on the IO thread.

For the fix, I think we should [unregister the lock]([link] before [unlocks other blocked locks]([link] So that whether an origin is accessed is updated before updating the SQL statement.

In this case, the quota might have been updated (decreased), for the padding part, but the actual deletion wouldn't have happened yet: if it fails, it will be triggered again on next try, and could result in the same value ended up being subtracted twice in the quota.

We should update the quota only if the operation completed successfully.

IDB large objects aren't stored directly in the sqlite file: they are stored as external files.

When doing so, [we first update the quota usage, then do the actual write]([link]

Unhandled error coupled to version change leads to initialization failure in xpcshell tests with conditioned profiles

When `CacheQuotaClient::InitOrigin()` is called during temporary storage initialization, it opens the origin's caches.sqlite and calls `CreateOrMigrateSchema()`. If the database has an incompatible schema version, e.g., from a different build or a future version that can't be downgraded, `Validate()` fails with `NS_ERROR_FAILURE`. This error is not caught by `IsDatabaseCorruptionError` in `InitializeOriginDirectory()` which only matches `NS_ERROR_FILE_CORRUPTED` and `NS_ERROR_STORAGE_IOERR`. The error propagates up and kills InitializeTemporaryStorageInternal(), causing FirstInitializationAttempt to record a permanent failure. All subsequent temporary storage operations fail immediately.

This manifests in CI with conditioned profiles (youtube.com, ebay.com origins) when the condprof was generated from a build whose cache schema version differs from the test build's `kLatestSchemaVersion` (31). 15+ dom/localstorage and 5+ dom/quota xpcshell tests are affected.

-> dom/cache/QuotaClient.cpp `GetTotalDiskUsageFromDB()` propagates
-> dom/cache/QuotaClient.cpp `CacheQuotaClient::InitOrigin()` propagates
-> dom/quota/ActorsParent.cpp `InitializeOrigin()` per-client error -> statusKeeper

-> dom/quota/ActorsParent.cpp `InitializeRepository()` statusKeeper returned
